correctness.rationale: The finite-n arclength intensity follows by coarea, independence and zero-length intersections. An explicit separation-lune parameterization proves q(theta,alpha)=theta*a(alpha)+O(theta^2) uniformly. The strictly positive density gives a global exponential integrable dominator, yielding L1 and total-variation convergence including normalization. Circular Fourier convolution has nonzero multipliers at every even harmonic, proving uniqueness; combining its mass identity with the leading mean perimeter determines the absolute trace. Strict Jensen gives the equality classification. Exact nonisotropic q and h were cross-checked by independent sphere integration and direct random cell geometry in verify_anisotropic.py.

originality.rationale: The accepted content is the joint polar-position/arclength Gamma mixture for the fixed-pole cell under anisotropic spherical normal distributions, with an equatorial-normal tomography formula and sharp perimeter extremal law. The most relevant 2020 nonisotropic spherical tessellation paper gives the directions of typical faces, not polar positions of boundary arclength relative to a fixed pole. The older isotropic zero-cell expected perimeter is expressly credited and excluded as a new contribution. No examined relevant primary statement implies the specific combined law. Historical priority remains provisional.
residual_risks: A differently indexed general anisotropic hyperplane zero-cell boundary functional could contain an equivalent consequence; no negative-search outcome proves historical uniqueness.
The classical invertibility of the circular cosine transform is known; priority is claimed only for its coupling to fixed-pole boundary statistics.
The same conclusion is not asserted for rough/vanishing densities or noisy inverse data.

value.rationale: The mathematical object is the arclength-weighted boundary geometry of a specified spherical cell, for which anisotropy changes not merely mean size but the joint distribution of distance and direction. The theorem identifies the universal conditional Gamma law, an explicit anisotropic angular bias, a sharp perimeter extremal theorem, and a nontrivial inverse problem: both limiting boundary observables recover the directional normal density along the equator. These statements answer natural geometric and inverse-sampling questions; they are not a numerical recomputation of an old isotropic constant.
